program_primer_markdown:
# AI for data engineers — program primer

You already know how to ship reliable data systems. This certificate applies the same habits to **LLM-powered** pipelines: contracts, tests, observability, and prove gates—without pretending you need a PhD in deep learning first.

## Mental model in one paragraph

An **LLM** is a probabilistic function: text in → text out. It does not “know” your warehouse schema. You wrap it with **schemas** (Pydantic), **retries**, **golden sets**, and a **gateway** (LiteLLM) the same way you wrap flaky APIs with idempotent jobs and SLAs.

## DE concept → AI platform concept

| You already do (data engineering) | AI systems analogue |
| --- | --- |
| Table schema + NOT NULL | Pydantic model + Instructor validation |
| dbt tests / Great Expectations | Golden-set evals + invariant checks |
| Airflow retry + alert | LLM retry on `ValidationError` + fallback model |
| Lineage (OpenLineage, column lineage) | Trace IDs across gateway, graph, tools |
| API gateway / rate limits | LiteLLM router, budgets, per-request cost log |
| Feature store / embeddings table | Vector index + hybrid (BM25 + dense) search |
| RBAC on tables | OPA policy on tools and MCP actions |
| CI on SQL changes | CI that blocks eval regression on PRs |
| Idempotent batch job | Checkpointed LangGraph run (resume after failure) |

## Prerequisites (honest)

- Comfortable **Python** (functions, classes, `pytest`)
- **Git** and a public GitHub repo for Prove gates
- Read/write **JSON** and env-based config
- Optional: Docker, one cloud account for deploy month

You do **not** need: training neural nets from scratch, CUDA, or completing every optional video.

## The capstone thread

Every course extends one story: **Autonomous Data Reconciliation Platform** (synthetic/public logs only).

| Phase | Courses | What you add to the repo |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Boot | 0 | Typed extraction + golden-set % |
| Gateway | 1 | LiteLLM + cost/latency logging |
| Orchestration | 2–3 | LangGraph + MCP tools + audit log |
| Retrieval | 4–6 | Hybrid search, chunks, one graph validator |
| Quality | 7–9 | Eval harness, CI gate, policy + traces |
| Ship | 10–12 | Integrated alpha, deploy doc, lineage sample |
| Career | 13–15 | Frontier slice, portfolio, interviews |

Open **Course 0 → Overview** for the month-by-month prove rubrics, then pick the first **Watch** topic.

## How to use this studio

1. **Course overview** — outcomes, concept map, prove acceptance table.
2. **Topic → Theory tab** — choose **Beginner**, **Intermediate**, or **Advanced** (every topic has all three).
3. **Lecture tab** — video or external course **after** theory feels clear.
4. **Lab & Prove** — paste artifact URL; you self-certify (no auto-grader).
5. **Regenerate** — optional AI rewrite (your API keys); saved per Google account on this browser.
6. **Mentor** — interview prompts and tradeoffs.

| Level | Best for |
| --- | --- |
| Beginner | New to AI; DE background; wants analogies and order |
| Intermediate | Default study guide, prove rubric, five layers |
| Advanced | Staff SLOs, tradeoffs, interview depth |

## First 90 minutes (if you are new to LLMs)

1. Skim this page.
2. Complete **Karpathy — Intro to LLMs** (Course 0) with three notes: tokens, context limit, one failure mode.
3. Read **Instructor quick start** — only “why structured output” sections.
4. Open your boot repo; add `.env.example` and a one-line `extract()` stub.

Mark topics complete when **this checkbox’s** objective is met—not when you finish entire playlists or doc sites.

glossary.definition: A chunk of text the model reads or generates; billing and context limits are counted in tokens.
glossary.de_analogy: Like rows or bytes processed—your cost and SLA driver.

glossary.definition: Maximum tokens the model can consider in one request (prompt + completion).
glossary.de_analogy: Like a max batch size—overflow means truncate, summarize, or chunk.

glossary.definition: Running a trained model to produce outputs (not training).
glossary.de_analogy: Running a scoring job in prod vs retraining the model.

glossary.definition: Model output that looks plausible but is factually wrong or unsupported.
glossary.de_analogy: Bad join or null handling that still returns a row—never trust without validation.

glossary.definition: Forcing LLM responses into a schema (JSON/Pydantic) instead of free text.
glossary.de_analogy: Contract-first API response types and schema enforcement.

glossary.definition: Python library for data validation and settings using type hints.
glossary.de_analogy: Runtime schema checks like Great Expectations on a single record.

glossary.definition: Library that pairs LLM calls with Pydantic models and retries on validation failure.
glossary.de_analogy: Retry loop around a flaky API until the payload passes JSON schema.

glossary.definition: Gateway that routes requests to many model providers with one API.
glossary.de_analogy: API gateway + provider failover for model endpoints.

glossary.definition: Central entry for models: auth, routing, budgets, logging, fallbacks.
glossary.de_analogy: Kong/Apigee-style layer before downstream services.

glossary.definition: Fixed labeled examples (input → expected output) used to score changes.
glossary.de_analogy: Fixture tables in dbt tests or regression datasets.

glossary.definition: Scripts/CI that run the golden set and report metrics on every change.
glossary.de_analogy: pytest + data diff job in CI.

glossary.definition: Business rule beyond JSON shape (e.g. balances sum to zero).
glossary.de_analogy: Custom SQL tests or domain constraints.

glossary.definition: Time to first token—latency until the model starts streaming output.
glossary.de_analogy: Time-to-first-byte on an API response.

glossary.definition: Retrieval-augmented generation: fetch relevant docs, then answer with the model.
glossary.de_analogy: Join to a reference table before computing a metric.

glossary.definition: Vector representation of text used for similarity search.
glossary.de_analogy: Feature vector for fuzzy matching instead of exact keys.

glossary.definition: Framework for agent workflows as graphs with state and checkpoints.
glossary.de_analogy: Airflow DAG with per-run state and human approval nodes.

glossary.definition: Persisted graph state so a run can resume after failure or interrupt.
glossary.de_analogy: Idempotent checkpoint in Spark/Flink or workflow saga state.

glossary.definition: Human-in-the-loop: pause automation for review before continuing.
glossary.de_analogy: Manual approval step in a pipeline.

glossary.definition: System that plans steps and calls tools; not just one LLM prompt.
glossary.de_analogy: Orchestrated micro-jobs with side effects—not a single SQL statement.

glossary.definition: Model Context Protocol—standard way to expose tools and resources to models.
glossary.de_analogy: Internal tool catalog + OpenAPI for agents.

glossary.definition: JSON schema describing parameters an agent tool accepts.
glossary.de_analogy: API request body contract.

glossary.definition: Append-only record of who invoked which tool with what outcome.
glossary.de_analogy: CloudTrail / data access logs for compliance.

glossary.definition: Metric got worse vs baseline on the golden set after a change.
glossary.de_analogy: CI test failure on main metrics.

glossary.definition: Secondary model or provider used when the primary fails or is slow.
glossary.de_analogy: Secondary region or read replica failover.

glossary.definition: How the model picks the next token (temperature, top-p).
glossary.de_analogy: Random seed / tie-break policy—lower temperature = more deterministic.

glossary.definition: Mechanism for the model to weigh which input tokens matter for each output token.
glossary.de_analogy: Weighted join keys—without math depth, just “focus mechanism.”

# Karpathy — Intro to LLMs

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

A plain-language tour of what LLMs are, how they are trained, and how inference works.

**Why it shows up now:** Before writing extraction code, you need a mental picture of tokens, context limits, and why models hallucinate.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **Token** — A chunk of text the model reads or generates; billing and context limits are counted in tokens.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Like rows or bytes processed—your cost and SLA driver.
- **Context window** — Maximum tokens the model can consider in one request (prompt + completion).
  - *Like in data engineering:* Like a max batch size—overflow means truncate, summarize, or chunk.
- **Inference** — Running a trained model to produce outputs (not training).
  - *Like in data engineering:* Running a scoring job in prod vs retraining the model.
- **Hallucination** — Model output that looks plausible but is factually wrong or unsupported.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Bad join or null handling that still returns a row—never trust without validation.

## Best order for this topic

1. Stay on **Beginner** (this page) until the ideas feel familiar.
2. Tap **Intermediate** for the full study guide and prove rubric.
3. Open the **Lecture** tab for video or the external course—pause and take notes.
4. Use **Lab & Prove** when you have something to link.

## When you watch, look for

- How text becomes tokens
- What the model sees at inference time
- Limits of memorization vs reasoning

## How this month fits together

Course **0** is building toward:
- Structured extraction with Instructor, Pydantic, LiteLLM, pytest
- Retry loops and invariant validators on messy logs
- OSS README with metrics and threat model

## Ready for the lecture when

You can explain to a data engineer what an LLM is without saying “AI magic.”

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

Short course on using Pydantic models so LLM outputs are typed JSON you can trust in pipelines.

**Why it shows up now:** Right after Karpathy intro—connects ‘messy text out’ to ‘schema-shaped data’ like a warehouse contract.

- **Structured output** — Forcing LLM responses into a schema (JSON/Pydantic) instead of free text.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Contract-first API response types and schema enforcement.
- **Invariant** — Business rule beyond JSON shape (e.g. balances sum to zero).

# Instructor — quick start

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

Library that forces LLM outputs into Pydantic models with retries on validation errors.

**Why it shows up now:** Boot week: your reconciler must return typed JSON, not free-form text.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **Structured output** — Forcing LLM responses into a schema (JSON/Pydantic) instead of free text.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Contract-first API response types and schema enforcement.
- **Pydantic** — Python library for data validation and settings using type hints.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Runtime schema checks like Great Expectations on a single record.
- **Golden set** — Fixed labeled examples (input → expected output) used to score changes.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Fixture tables in dbt tests or regression datasets.

## Best order for this topic

1. Stay on **Beginner** (this page) until the ideas feel familiar.
2. Tap **Intermediate** for the full study guide and prove rubric.
3. Open the **Lecture** tab for video or the external course—pause and take notes.
4. Use **Lab & Prove** when you have something to link.

## When you read, skim these parts first

- Quick start
- Retries
- Partial validation

## How this month fits together

Course **0** is building toward:
- Structured extraction with Instructor, Pydantic, LiteLLM, pytest
- Retry loops and invariant validators on messy logs
- OSS README with metrics and threat model

## Ready for the lecture when

Golden set reports valid JSON % on `data/golden/`.

# LiteLLM — reliable completions / fallbacks

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

Fallback chains and reliability patterns when a provider rate-limits or errors.

**Why it shows up now:** After single-model extraction works, production needs failover—not a 3am pages for 429s.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **LiteLLM** — Gateway that routes requests to many model providers with one API.
  - *Like in data engineering:* API gateway + provider failover for model endpoints.
- **Model fallback** — Secondary model or provider used when the primary fails or is slow.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Secondary region or read replica failover.
- **LLM gateway** — Central entry for models: auth, routing, budgets, logging, fallbacks.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Kong/Apigee-style layer before downstream services.

## Best order for this topic

1. Stay on **Beginner** (this page) until the ideas feel familiar.
2. Tap **Intermediate** for the full study guide and prove rubric.
3. Open the **Lecture** tab for video or the external course—pause and take notes.
4. Use **Lab & Prove** when you have something to link.

## When you read, skim these parts first

- Reliable completions
- Fallbacks
- Timeouts

## How this month fits together

Course **0** is building toward:
- Structured extraction with Instructor, Pydantic, LiteLLM, pytest
- Retry loops and invariant validators on messy logs
- OSS README with metrics and threat model

# Hamel — evals intro

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

How to think about evals: golden sets, tiers, and what to measure before launch.

**Why it shows up now:** Introduces the eval mindset used again in Courses 7–8 (harness + CI).

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **Golden set** — Fixed labeled examples (input → expected output) used to score changes.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Fixture tables in dbt tests or regression datasets.
- **Eval harness** — Scripts/CI that run the golden set and report metrics on every change.

- **Eval harness** — Scripts/CI that run the golden set and report metrics on every change.
  - *Like in data engineering:* pytest + data diff job in CI.

# Karpathy — Deep Dive into LLMs

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

Deep dive into transformers, KV cache, and how chat models run in production.

**Why it shows up now:** Course 1 connects gateway cost and latency to what actually happens inside the model stack.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **Inference** — Running a trained model to produce outputs (not training).
  - *Like in data engineering:* Running a scoring job in prod vs retraining the model.
- **Token** — A chunk of text the model reads or generates; billing and context limits are counted in tokens.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Like rows or bytes processed—your cost and SLA driver.
- **TTFT** — Time to first token—latency until the model starts streaming output.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Time-to-first-byte on an API response.
- **Attention** — Mechanism for the model to weigh which input tokens matter for each output token.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Weighted join keys—without math depth, just “focus mechanism.”
- **Sampling** — How the model picks the next token (temperature, top-p).
  - *Like in data engineering:* Random seed / tie-break policy—lower temperature = more deterministic.

## Best order for this topic

1. Stay on **Beginner** (this page) until the ideas feel familiar.
2. Tap **Intermediate** for the full study guide and prove rubric.
3. Open the **Lecture** tab for video or the external course—pause and take notes.
4. Use **Lab & Prove** when you have something to link.

## When you watch, look for

- Transformer block at a high level
- Why context length matters for cost
- Sampling knobs (temperature)

Course **1** is building toward:
- LLM lifecycle, limits, and interview-ready mental models
- Free **DL.AI / YouTube** LLM foundations (time-boxed)
- LiteLLM cost logging and CLI hardening

lessons.content:
## 🏗️ Architectural Overview
A typical GPT model uses a decoder-only transformer architecture. 

### Core Components:
1. **Token Embeddings:** Maps vocabulary to dense vectors.
2. **Positional Encoding:** Injects sequence order.
3. **Self-Attention Blocks:** Captures relationships.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.nn import functional as F

class Head(nn.Module):
    \"\"\" one head of self-attention \"\"\"
    def __init__(self, head_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.key = nn.Linear(n_embd, head_size, bias=False)
        self.query = nn.Linear(n_embd, head_size, bias=False)
        self.value = nn.Linear(n_embd, head_size, bias=False)
        self.register_buffer("tril", torch.tril(torch.ones(block_size, block_size)))

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        k = self.key(x)   
        q = self.query(x) 
        wei = q @ k.transpose(-2,-1) * C**-0.5 
        wei = wei.masked_fill(self.tril[:T, :T] == 0, float("-inf"))
        wei = F.softmax(wei, dim=-1)
        v = self.value(x) 
        return wei @ v 
```

### 🧠 Mathematical Intuition
$$ \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V $$

### 🛡️ Production Invariants
- Always enforce `B, T, C` tensor shape contracts.
- Apply `torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_` to prevent gradient explosion.

# LiteLLM docs hub

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

Fallback chains and reliability patterns when a provider rate-limits or errors.

**Why it shows up now:** After single-model extraction works, production needs failover—not a 3am pages for 429s.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **LiteLLM** — Gateway that routes requests to many model providers with one API.
  - *Like in data engineering:* API gateway + provider failover for model endpoints.
- **Model fallback** — Secondary model or provider used when the primary fails or is slow.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Secondary region or read replica failover.
- **LLM gateway** — Central entry for models: auth, routing, budgets, logging, fallbacks.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Kong/Apigee-style layer before downstream services.

## Best order for this topic

1. Stay on **Beginner** (this page) until the ideas feel familiar.
2. Tap **Intermediate** for the full study guide and prove rubric.

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

Fallback chains and reliability patterns when a provider rate-limits or errors.

**Why it shows up now:** After single-model extraction works, production needs failover—not a 3am pages for 429s.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **LiteLLM** — Gateway that routes requests to many model providers with one API.
  - *Like in data engineering:* API gateway + provider failover for model endpoints.
- **Model fallback** — Secondary model or provider used when the primary fails or is slow.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Secondary region or read replica failover.
- **LLM gateway** — Central entry for models: auth, routing, budgets, logging, fallbacks.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Kong/Apigee-style layer before downstream services.

# AI Agents in LangGraph

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

State-machine orchestration for agents: nodes, edges, checkpoints, human interrupts.

**Why it shows up now:** Course 2 wraps your reconciler in a graph with HITL on validation failure.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **Structured output** — Forcing LLM responses into a schema (JSON/Pydantic) instead of free text.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Contract-first API response types and schema enforcement.
- **Inference** — Running a trained model to produce outputs (not training).
  - *Like in data engineering:* Running a scoring job in prod vs retraining the model.
- **LangGraph** — Framework for agent workflows as graphs with state and checkpoints.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Airflow DAG with per-run state and human approval nodes.
- **Checkpoint** — Persisted graph state so a run can resume after failure or interrupt.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Idempotent checkpoint in Spark/Flink or workflow saga state.
- **HITL** — Human-in-the-loop: pause automation for review before continuing.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Manual approval step in a pipeline.
- **Agent** — System that plans steps and calls tools; not just one LLM prompt.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Orchestrated micro-jobs with side effects—not a single SQL statement.

## Best order for this topic

1. Stay on **Beginner** (this page) until the ideas feel familiar.
2. Tap **Intermediate** for the full study guide and prove rubric.
3. Open the **Lecture** tab for video or the external course—pause and take notes.
4. Use **Lab & Prove** when you have something to link.

## When you watch, look for

- Definitions in plain language (pause and write them down)
- One production constraint the speaker mentions
- One failure mode or ‘don’t do this’ moment
- How this connects to typed extraction, agents, or evals

Course **2** is building toward:

- LangChain vs LangGraph tradeoffs (interview narrative)
- Reconciler wrapped in LangGraph

- **Structured output** — Forcing LLM responses into a schema (JSON/Pydantic) instead of free text.

- **Inference** — Running a trained model to produce outputs (not training).

- **LangGraph** — Framework for agent workflows as graphs with state and checkpoints.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Airflow DAG with per-run state and human approval nodes.
- **Checkpoint** — Persisted graph state so a run can resume after failure or interrupt.

- **Agent** — System that plans steps and calls tools; not just one LLM prompt.

- Unlike linear DAGs (LangChain classic), LangGraph models agent loops as cyclic state graphs with explicit memory nodes and routing edges.

- Creating infinite agent loops without a maximum iteration guard or step counter.
- Passing large payloads inside state instead of storing artifacts in S3 and passing pointers.

# Document Chat RAG walkthrough

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

Video lesson—capture diagrams and production constraints, not full transcript notes.

**Why it shows up now:** Builds interview-ready intuition before you automate the pattern in code.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **Agent** — System that plans steps and calls tools; not just one LLM prompt.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Orchestrated micro-jobs with side effects—not a single SQL statement.
- **LangGraph** — Framework for agent workflows as graphs with state and checkpoints.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Airflow DAG with per-run state and human approval nodes.
- **Embedding** — Vector representation of text used for similarity search.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Feature vector for fuzzy matching instead of exact keys.
- **Attention** — Mechanism for the model to weigh which input tokens matter for each output token.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Weighted join keys—without math depth, just “focus mechanism.”
- **Structured output** — Forcing LLM responses into a schema (JSON/Pydantic) instead of free text.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Contract-first API response types and schema enforcement.
- **Inference** — Running a trained model to produce outputs (not training).
  - *Like in data engineering:* Running a scoring job in prod vs retraining the model.

## Best order for this topic

1. Stay on **Beginner** (this page) until the ideas feel familiar.
2. Tap **Intermediate** for the full study guide and prove rubric.
3. Open the **Lecture** tab for video or the external course—pause and take notes.
4. Use **Lab & Prove** when you have something to link.

## When you watch, look for

- Definitions
- Failure modes
- What would you monitor in prod

## How this month fits together

Course **4** is building toward:
- Dense + sparse (BM25) + **RRF** fusion
- recall@k on labeled questions
- Retrieval as agent tool (not chat-only RAG)

## Ready for the lecture when

You can explain the main idea in under two minutes aloud.

# Docling (IBM)

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

Video lesson—capture diagrams and production constraints, not full transcript notes.

**Why it shows up now:** Builds interview-ready intuition before you automate the pattern in code.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **Agent** — System that plans steps and calls tools; not just one LLM prompt.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Orchestrated micro-jobs with side effects—not a single SQL statement.
- **LangGraph** — Framework for agent workflows as graphs with state and checkpoints.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Airflow DAG with per-run state and human approval nodes.
- **Embedding** — Vector representation of text used for similarity search.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Feature vector for fuzzy matching instead of exact keys.
- **Attention** — Mechanism for the model to weigh which input tokens matter for each output token.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Weighted join keys—without math depth, just “focus mechanism.”
- **Structured output** — Forcing LLM responses into a schema (JSON/Pydantic) instead of free text.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Contract-first API response types and schema enforcement.
- **Inference** — Running a trained model to produce outputs (not training).
  - *Like in data engineering:* Running a scoring job in prod vs retraining the model.

1. Stay on **Beginner** (this page) until the ideas feel familiar.

- **Embedding** — Vector representation of text used for similarity search.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Feature vector for fuzzy matching instead of exact keys.
- **Tool schema** — JSON schema describing parameters an agent tool accepts.

- **MCP** — Model Context Protocol—standard way to expose tools and resources to models.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Internal tool catalog + OpenAPI for agents.
- **Sampling** — How the model picks the next token (temperature, top-p).
  - *Like in data engineering:* Random seed / tie-break policy—lower temperature = more deterministic.

# DeepEval — CI/CD

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

Documentation reading—extract APIs and decisions, not every paragraph.

**Why it shows up now:** Maps directly to adopt / experiment / defer choices on the capstone.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **Golden set** — Fixed labeled examples (input → expected output) used to score changes.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Fixture tables in dbt tests or regression datasets.
- **RAG** — Retrieval-augmented generation: fetch relevant docs, then answer with the model.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Join to a reference table before computing a metric.
- **Embedding** — Vector representation of text used for similarity search.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Feature vector for fuzzy matching instead of exact keys.
- **Tool schema** — JSON schema describing parameters an agent tool accepts.
  - *Like in data engineering:* API request body contract.
- **MCP** — Model Context Protocol—standard way to expose tools and resources to models.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Internal tool catalog + OpenAPI for agents.
- **Sampling** — How the model picks the next token (temperature, top-p).
  - *Like in data engineering:* Random seed / tie-break policy—lower temperature = more deterministic.

## Best order for this topic

1. Stay on **Beginner** (this page) until the ideas feel familiar.
2. Tap **Intermediate** for the full study guide and prove rubric.

# Open Policy Agent docs

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

Documentation reading—extract APIs and decisions, not every paragraph.

**Why it shows up now:** Maps directly to adopt / experiment / defer choices on the capstone.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **Audit log** — Append-only record of who invoked which tool with what outcome.
  - *Like in data engineering:* CloudTrail / data access logs for compliance.
- **Golden set** — Fixed labeled examples (input → expected output) used to score changes.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Fixture tables in dbt tests or regression datasets.
- **RAG** — Retrieval-augmented generation: fetch relevant docs, then answer with the model.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Join to a reference table before computing a metric.
- **Embedding** — Vector representation of text used for similarity search.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Feature vector for fuzzy matching instead of exact keys.
- **Tool schema** — JSON schema describing parameters an agent tool accepts.
  - *Like in data engineering:* API request body contract.
- **MCP** — Model Context Protocol—standard way to expose tools and resources to models.

# LangGraph: pass → stage write; fail → `interrupt()` HITL

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

State-machine orchestration for agents: nodes, edges, checkpoints, human interrupts.

**Why it shows up now:** Course 2 wraps your reconciler in a graph with HITL on validation failure.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **Structured output** — Forcing LLM responses into a schema (JSON/Pydantic) instead of free text.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Contract-first API response types and schema enforcement.
- **Inference** — Running a trained model to produce outputs (not training).
  - *Like in data engineering:* Running a scoring job in prod vs retraining the model.
- **LangGraph** — Framework for agent workflows as graphs with state and checkpoints.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Airflow DAG with per-run state and human approval nodes.
- **Checkpoint** — Persisted graph state so a run can resume after failure or interrupt.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Idempotent checkpoint in Spark/Flink or workflow saga state.
- **HITL** — Human-in-the-loop: pause automation for review before continuing.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Manual approval step in a pipeline.
- **Agent** — System that plans steps and calls tools; not just one LLM prompt.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Orchestrated micro-jobs with side effects—not a single SQL statement.

# LiteLLM prompt caching

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

Fallback chains and reliability patterns when a provider rate-limits or errors.

**Why it shows up now:** After single-model extraction works, production needs failover—not a 3am pages for 429s.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **Agent** — System that plans steps and calls tools; not just one LLM prompt.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Orchestrated micro-jobs with side effects—not a single SQL statement.
- **LangGraph** — Framework for agent workflows as graphs with state and checkpoints.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Airflow DAG with per-run state and human approval nodes.
- **TTFT** — Time to first token—latency until the model starts streaming output.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Time-to-first-byte on an API response.
- **LiteLLM** — Gateway that routes requests to many model providers with one API.
  - *Like in data engineering:* API gateway + provider failover for model endpoints.
- **Model fallback** — Secondary model or provider used when the primary fails or is slow.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Secondary region or read replica failover.
- **LLM gateway** — Central entry for models: auth, routing, budgets, logging, fallbacks.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Kong/Apigee-style layer before downstream services.

1. Stay on **Beginner** (this page) until the ideas feel familiar.

# Ingest → gateway (caching on) → extract → validate → LangGraph → stage DB

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

State-machine orchestration for agents: nodes, edges, checkpoints, human interrupts.

**Why it shows up now:** Course 2 wraps your reconciler in a graph with HITL on validation failure.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **Structured output** — Forcing LLM responses into a schema (JSON/Pydantic) instead of free text.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Contract-first API response types and schema enforcement.
- **Inference** — Running a trained model to produce outputs (not training).
  - *Like in data engineering:* Running a scoring job in prod vs retraining the model.
- **LangGraph** — Framework for agent workflows as graphs with state and checkpoints.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Airflow DAG with per-run state and human approval nodes.
- **Checkpoint** — Persisted graph state so a run can resume after failure or interrupt.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Idempotent checkpoint in Spark/Flink or workflow saga state.
- **HITL** — Human-in-the-loop: pause automation for review before continuing.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Manual approval step in a pipeline.
- **Agent** — System that plans steps and calls tools; not just one LLM prompt.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Orchestrated micro-jobs with side effects—not a single SQL statement.

# Kubernetes Community

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

Video lesson—capture diagrams and production constraints, not full transcript notes.

**Why it shows up now:** Builds interview-ready intuition before you automate the pattern in code.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **RAG** — Retrieval-augmented generation: fetch relevant docs, then answer with the model.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Join to a reference table before computing a metric.
- **Golden set** — Fixed labeled examples (input → expected output) used to score changes.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Fixture tables in dbt tests or regression datasets.
- **Eval harness** — Scripts/CI that run the golden set and report metrics on every change.
  - *Like in data engineering:* pytest + data diff job in CI.
- **LLM gateway** — Central entry for models: auth, routing, budgets, logging, fallbacks.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Kong/Apigee-style layer before downstream services.
- **Agent** — System that plans steps and calls tools; not just one LLM prompt.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Orchestrated micro-jobs with side effects—not a single SQL statement.
- **LangGraph** — Framework for agent workflows as graphs with state and checkpoints.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Airflow DAG with per-run state and human approval nodes.

## Best order for this topic

1. Stay on **Beginner** (this page) until the ideas feel familiar.
2. Tap **Intermediate** for the full study guide and prove rubric.

# LiteLLM proxy server

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

Fallback chains and reliability patterns when a provider rate-limits or errors.

**Why it shows up now:** After single-model extraction works, production needs failover—not a 3am pages for 429s.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **Agent** — System that plans steps and calls tools; not just one LLM prompt.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Orchestrated micro-jobs with side effects—not a single SQL statement.
- **LangGraph** — Framework for agent workflows as graphs with state and checkpoints.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Airflow DAG with per-run state and human approval nodes.
- **TTFT** — Time to first token—latency until the model starts streaming output.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Time-to-first-byte on an API response.
- **LiteLLM** — Gateway that routes requests to many model providers with one API.
  - *Like in data engineering:* API gateway + provider failover for model endpoints.
- **Model fallback** — Secondary model or provider used when the primary fails or is slow.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Secondary region or read replica failover.
- **LLM gateway** — Central entry for models: auth, routing, budgets, logging, fallbacks.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Kong/Apigee-style layer before downstream services.

## Best order for this topic

1. Stay on **Beginner** (this page) until the ideas feel familiar.
2. Tap **Intermediate** for the full study guide and prove rubric.
3. Open the **Lecture** tab for video or the external course—pause and take notes.

# **vLLM** — docs · local model behind LiteLLM

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

Fallback chains and reliability patterns when a provider rate-limits or errors.

**Why it shows up now:** After single-model extraction works, production needs failover—not a 3am pages for 429s.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **Inference** — Running a trained model to produce outputs (not training).
  - *Like in data engineering:* Running a scoring job in prod vs retraining the model.
- **Agent** — System that plans steps and calls tools; not just one LLM prompt.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Orchestrated micro-jobs with side effects—not a single SQL statement.
- **LangGraph** — Framework for agent workflows as graphs with state and checkpoints.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Airflow DAG with per-run state and human approval nodes.
- **TTFT** — Time to first token—latency until the model starts streaming output.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Time-to-first-byte on an API response.
- **LiteLLM** — Gateway that routes requests to many model providers with one API.
  - *Like in data engineering:* API gateway + provider failover for model endpoints.
- **Model fallback** — Secondary model or provider used when the primary fails or is slow.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Secondary region or read replica failover.

## Best order for this topic

1. Stay on **Beginner** (this page) until the ideas feel familiar.
2. Tap **Intermediate** for the full study guide and prove rubric.
3. Open the **Lecture** tab for video or the external course—pause and take notes.
4. Use **Lab & Prove** when you have something to link.

## How this month fits together

Course **13** is building toward:
- How to pick and time-box one frontier track (inference, DSPy, caching, or semantic cache)
- How to wire a local or gateway-backed experiment with before/after metrics
- How to document bottleneck, metric, and “why we added X” for staff review

## Ready for the lecture when

README shows one forced failure switching to fallback successfully.

# Unsloth

> **Beginner path** — no prior AI background assumed. Read this, then use the **Lecture** tab when you feel oriented.

## What is this, in plain English?

Documentation reading—extract APIs and decisions, not every paragraph.

**Why it shows up now:** Maps directly to adopt / experiment / defer choices on the capstone.

## Words you will hear (simple meanings)

- **TTFT** — Time to first token—latency until the model starts streaming output.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Time-to-first-byte on an API response.
- **Audit log** — Append-only record of who invoked which tool with what outcome.
  - *Like in data engineering:* CloudTrail / data access logs for compliance.
- **Golden set** — Fixed labeled examples (input → expected output) used to score changes.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Fixture tables in dbt tests or regression datasets.
- **RAG** — Retrieval-augmented generation: fetch relevant docs, then answer with the model.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Join to a reference table before computing a metric.
- **Embedding** — Vector representation of text used for similarity search.
  - *Like in data engineering:* Feature vector for fuzzy matching instead of exact keys.
- **Tool schema** — JSON schema describing parameters an agent tool accepts.
  - *Like in data engineering:* API request body contract.

## Best order for this topic

1. Stay on **Beginner** (this page) until the ideas feel familiar.
2. Tap **Intermediate** for the full study guide and prove rubric.

- **Embedding** — Vector representation of text used for similarity search. _DE angle:_ Feature vector for fuzzy matching instead of exact keys.
- **Tool schema** — JSON schema describing parameters an agent tool accepts. _DE angle:_ API request body contract.
